item.title: A poker rating that ignores whether you won the hand
item.description: The Pip Rating grades each call, fold and opening move on the cards you could see, so a bad beat costs nothing. 1,000 gives away 2.5% of what was at stake, and every halving is 350 points. Calling everything and folding everything both rate about 400. What the server checks, and what it cannot.
item.content:encoded:
The problem with counting wins

Poker results are mostly the cards. You can play a hand perfectly and lose it, and play it badly and win, and over an evening the cards can hide which of those you did. A rating built on who won would mostly be a rating of luck.

The Pip Rating ignores who won. It looks at each decision when you made it, with the cards you could see, and asks how much that decision gave away against the other choice. A right call that loses to a river card costs you nothing. A bad call that gets lucky still costs what it cost.

What it grades

Two kinds of decision. Every call or fold you make facing a bet, priced in big blinds from your equity and the price you were offered. And your first move when it folds round to you before the flop, graded against the two charts the app already teaches: the shove chart when you have 15 big blinds or fewer, the opening chart from 25.

It does not grade bets and raises after the flop. What they are worth depends on how often the other player folds, and the only players we could measure that against are Pip’s own. A rating built on that would reward beating our AI, which is not the same thing as playing well. The hand review still grades those, with every card face up.

It counts Hold’em hands at the ladder, the Rail, the Daily, the freeroll and the Hold’em side tables. Not the other variants, not drills, and not rooms with friends, for now.

The scale

Each decision has a stake (the pot plus the price) and a cost (what it gave up, at most 20 big blinds). Your rating comes from the share of the stake you gave away, over roughly your last 300 decisions, with recent ones counting more.

Give away 2.5% and you rate 1,000. Every time you halve that, you gain 350 points: 1.25% is 1,350, 0.625% is 1,700. Double it and you lose 350: 5% is 650.

Weighting by stake is what stops the obvious trick. Fold everything and you make hundreds of cheap, correct folds, but the few expensive ones you get wrong carry the weight.

The bands are Learning (under 800), Steady (800), Solid (1,200), Strong (1,600), Expert (2,000), Master (2,400).

Where people land

We seated scripted players at real tables against each table’s own AI and rated their hands exactly as the app does, a few hundred rated decisions each, so each figure is give or take about 100. Calling every bet rated about 400. So did folding to every bet, and so did calling or folding on a coin flip. Paying everything and paying nothing land in the same place.

The best player we could script, which plays the shove chart exactly, rated 1,670 to 2,160. So 2,000 sits at about the edge of the best play Pip has, and most people will never see it. That is on purpose. Nobody reaches 2,000 in chess in a month either.

Those scripted players decide with the same equity estimate that grades them, so they agree with the grader more than a person would. Real players will sit lower than their script. We would guess a careful beginner starts somewhere around 600 to 900, and we will know more once enough people have played.

New players

Everyone starts at 1,000. The rating is provisional until 50 rated decisions. After that the number is held under 1,600 until 300 decisions, under 2,000 until 1,000, and under 2,400 until 2,500. A good week is not a career. Your play still counts in full underneath, so the number catches up when a cap lifts, and the app tells you when one is holding you back.

What the server can and cannot check

Hands against the AI are dealt and played on your device. The server never sees a hand, only the list of decisions and what each cost. Someone determined could send decisions that never happened, and no check can prove otherwise.

What it can do is make that slow and visible. It works the rating out again itself rather than trusting the number your device sends. It refuses decisions that cost more than they could, hands less than two seconds apart, hands it has already counted, and more than900 decisions an hour. Once you are rated, one batch of hands moves you at most 60 points. And a record of 2,600 or better after 200 decisions comes off the leaderboard until a person has looked at it.

Someone patient enough can still beat that. If it becomes a problem, the fix is to rate only hands our server deals, which is how rooms with friends already work.

Who sees what

The number is free for everyone. Make an account and you are on the leaderboard, and you can take yourself off it at any time without your rating stopping. It is the one ranking on Pip anyone else can see. Your chips and your Roll title stay private.

Nothing you can buy raises it, because it measures decisions, and more tables or more chips do not make a call any better. What members get is the rating drawn day by day, and which kinds of decision are moving it. The number tells you where you are. The breakdown tells you which of your folds is doing it.

How we counted

The arithmetic is one file, src/lib/rating/maths.ts, and the server runs an exact copy of it. The opening and shove grades are src/lib/rating/preflop.ts. The scripted players are scripts/rating-calibrate.ts, run on 5 November 2026, and docs/rating.md has the full table and everything the server checks. Every figure on this page except the calibration comes from the code at build time, so if the scale changes, this page changes with it.

item.title: Set mining needs a deep stack. How long each table gives you one
item.description: A pocket pair flops its third card 2,304 times in 19,600, so calling a raise to three big blinds needs about 26 big blinds behind, on both sides, to break even. Pip’s ladder tables keep that for 18 to 20 hands. Deep Stack keeps it for 60 to 84. Counted from each table’s own blinds.
item.content:encoded:
The call

Set mining is calling a raise with a small pair for one reason: to flop three of a kind. If the flop misses, you fold. If it hits, you hope somebody has a hand they like.

The flop brings your third card 2,304 times in 19,600 (how often you flop a set has the full count). The other 17,296 times it does not. That is 7.5 misses for every hit, and every miss costs the call.

What the hit has to win

Say the raise is to 3 big blinds. Each miss costs 3, so to break even each hit has to win back 7.5 of those, about 23 big blinds, on top of the 3 it cost. Call it 26 big blinds in front of you.

The raiser needs them too. You can only win what they have, so the number that counts is the smaller of the two stacks.

And 26 is the floor. It assumes every set wins and every raiser pays you all of it. Sets lose, and people fold. The real number is higher, but nobody can tell you by how much without knowing who you are playing.

How long a table keeps 26 big blinds

In a tournament the blinds go up, so the same stack is worth fewer big blinds every level. Here is how many hands each of Pip’s tables deals before the stack you sat down with is under 26 big blinds, with the ladder table and Deep Stack at the same buy-in side by side.

  • 750 chips: The Pool Hall starts you at 75 big blinds and keeps 26 for 20 hands. Deep Stack starts you at 225 and keeps it for 72.
  • 2,000 chips: The Card Room starts you at 67 big blinds and keeps 26 for 18 hands. Deep Stack starts you at 200 and keeps it for 60.
  • 5,000 chips: Downtown Casino starts you at 100 big blinds and keeps 26 for 18 hands. Deep Stack starts you at 300 and keeps it for 84.
  • 15,000 chips: The Riverboat starts you at 100 big blinds and keeps 26 for 18 hands. Deep Stack starts you at 300 and keeps it for 84.
  • 40,000 chips: The Penthouse starts you at 100 big blinds and keeps 26 for 18 hands. Deep Stack starts you at 300 and keeps it for 84.

The ladder gives you 18 to 20 hands of set mining. Deep Stack gives you 60 to 84, more than three times as many at every price. With three times the chips and the same opening blinds, the blinds have to climb three times as high before the stack runs short, and Deep Stack’s levels last twelve hands at every price.

What this does not count

It counts the stack you sat down with. Win a pot and you are deeper than this, lose one and you are shorter, and the raiser’s stack moves the same way. Nor does anyone at the table promise to raise to 3 big blinds. Treat the numbers as a clock, not a forecast: they say when the blinds alone stop the call paying, and nothing about your cards.

How we counted

src/config/setMining.ts takes the flop count from the same file the set guide prints it from, and walks each table’s blinds hand by hand through src/config/blinds.ts, which is what the tables post their blinds with. tests/setMining.test.ts deals every flop again to recount the 2,304, and checks every figure on this page. Change a table’s blinds and this page changes with it, or the build fails.

Where it is

Deep Stack is a side table in the membership, at five prices from 750 to 40,000. The ladder stays free, and so does folding your sevens.

item.title: Calling a river bet: when the answer depends on who is betting
item.description: A bet of half the pot needs you to win one time in four, and a pot-sized bet one in three. Whether your pair does depends on how often they bluff. We dealt 40,000 hands through Pip’s river drill: about one river decision in four is right against one player and wrong against another.
item.content:encoded:
The short version

They bet the river. You have a pair. Calling costs a share of the pot you would win, and your hand has to win at least that often to be worth it. A bet of half the pot needs 25%. A bet of the pot needs 33.3%.

That half is arithmetic. The other half is how often your pair wins against the hands that bet like this, and that depends on how many of those bets are bluffs. We dealt 40,000 hands through Pip’s river drill to see how often that changes the answer. In 39,746 of 157,878 river decisions, it did.

The price

A call wins the pot plus their bet, and it costs your bet. So the share you pay is the bet over the pot plus both bets. The bigger the bet, the more often you need to win:

  • A bet of a fifth of the pot: you need to win 14.3%
  • A bet of a third of the pot: you need to win 20%
  • A bet of half the pot: you need to win 25%
  • A bet of three-quarters of the pot: you need to win 30%
  • A bet of the pot: you need to win 33.3%
  • A bet of twice the pot: you need to win 40%

None of this depends on who is betting. Everything after it does.

Who is betting

Pip’s river drill reads a bet as two kinds of hand. Value: the stronger half of the made hands they could have, or the strongest third when the bet is more than two-thirds of the pot. And bluffs: hands that missed, counted at a weight, because they bet some of those and not all of them.

The weight is the one number nobody can know about a stranger. So the drill prices every spot twice, once at the rate Pip’s AI players at Friends’ Garage bluff, the bottom of the ladder, and once at The Main Event’s, the top, where they bluff a good deal more. Those rates were measured from the AI players’ own river bets, not chosen.

What we found

Of 40,000 shuffles, 13,294 left you with a hand you would have played and a pair or better of your own on the river. Each was priced at twelve bet sizes, from a fifth of the pot to twice it: 157,878 different decisions. In 39,746 of them the call was right against one of those two players and wrong against the other.

That share hardly moves with the size of the bet. Out of 13,294 hands, it is between 2,830 and 4,053 at every size. What moves is the rest. Facing a fifth of the pot, the call was right against both players 6,530 times and wrong against both 3,139 times. Facing twice the pot, it was right against both 3,041 times and wrong against both 7,241.

Some of that is the price, and some is that the drill assumes a big bet is a stronger hand. Either way the lesson is a dull one. Against a small bet a pair is right to call about twice as often as it is right to fold, against a big one the other way round, and about one time in four the hand in front of you is not what decides it. The player is.

What the drill does about it

It leaves those out. A spot is only asked when the answer is the same against both players, and clear of the line by four points at each end. 1,033 of the 40,000 shuffles became a question. So the drill never marks you wrong for a call that was right against the other player.

A real table does not leave them out. There, knowing who bluffs is your job, and the price is the only part anybody can work out for you.

How we counted

src/lib/drills/riverBluffCount.ts deals the drill’s own spots, the same deal and prices the drill grades, and sorts each bet into right to call, right to fold, or depends. The model of what bets is src/lib/drills/riverRange.ts, where the measured bluffing rates are written down. The counts on this page are in src/config/riverBluffs.ts, and tests/riverBluffCount.test.ts counts them again on every build.

Every win share is exact against the model: each hand they could hold is compared with yours once. They are counts over a model of what bets, not over hands people played. Boards that make two pair on their own are left out, as the drill leaves them out.

Where it is

Calling the river is a drill in the membership. The page that link opens deals one spot from it. What have you got? and Which hand wins? stay free, with the ladder, the Rail, the Daily and the freeroll.

item.title: The most you can bet in Pot-Limit Omaha
item.description: You may raise by the size of the pot after you call. At 25 and 50 blinds the first raise is 175, then 600, 2,050 and 7,000, and the fifth is all-in from 200 big blinds. The shortcut players use, why it is out by a blind for the blinds, and the flop.
item.content:encoded:
Raise the pot, after you call

In Pot-Limit Omaha the most you can bet is the pot. That part is easy. The part people stop and count on their fingers is raising: you may raise by the size of the pot after you have called. Put the call in, look at the pot, and raise by that much.

Every number below is from The Big Pot, Pip’s Omaha table: 6 seats, 10,000 chips each, blinds of 25 and 50 to start. None of them were worked out by hand. They are what the table itself lets you put in.

The first raise

Before the flop the pot is the two blinds, 75. The first player to act calls 50, which makes it 125, and raises by that: 175 in all. Three and a half big blinds, which is the number to remember.

Everybody re-raises

Now let every player in turn raise as much as they are allowed.

  • Under the gun: to 175, the first raise
  • Hijack: to 600
  • Cutoff: to 2,050
  • Button: to 7,000
  • Small blind: all-in for 10,000

The fifth raise is the whole stack. The pot would allow more, and there is no more. 200 big blinds sounds deep until four people have raised the pot.

The shortcut, and the blind it misses

The sum players do in their heads is three times the bet you face, plus whatever was in before it. The hijack faces 175 with 75 of blinds behind it: three times 175 is 525, plus 75, is 600. Right.

For a blind it is out by the blind. Fold round to the big blind instead and it faces the same 175, but 50 of the pot is already its own, and the call is only 125. The most it may make it is 550, not 600. So: three times the bet, plus what was in before it, less what you already put in on this street.

After the flop

Say the first raise is called by the big blind and everyone else folds. The flop pot is 375, and the big blind, first to act, may bet 375: the pot, since there is nothing to call. Raising that is the shortcut again with nothing of yours in yet, three bets and the pot, which is 1,500.

A pot that starts at 375 can be 2,250 before anyone has called anything on the flop. Pot limit is a limit. It does not feel like one for long.

How we counted

The rule lives in one function in src/lib/poker/engine.ts, the engine that deals every hand at The Big Pot and at The Split, Pip’s Omaha Hi-Lo table, which is pot-limit too. src/config/potLimit.ts plays the hands above through that engine and prints what it allows, and tests/potLimit.test.ts checks the shortcut against every one of them. So this page cannot print a number the table would refuse, and the shortcut cannot drift from the table without the build failing.

You do not have to do the sum at the table. The Max button on the bet slider is the pot limit, or your stack if that is smaller.

Where it is

The Big Pot and The Split are side tables in the membership. The ladder, the Rail, the Daily and the freeroll stay free, and so does the arithmetic.

item.title: The house edge in Blackjack when you can only hit or stand
item.description: Pip’s Blackjack has no doubling and no splitting, and each table states its house edge. We played 40 million hands a table to check: one card was right and two said the house took more than it does. The numbers, what each rule is worth, and the whole strategy in a paragraph.
item.content:encoded:
The numbers on the cards

Pip’s Blackjack has two buttons, hit and stand. There is no doubling, no splitting and no surrender. Each of the three tables states its house edge on the card before you sit down, because a number you have to work out for yourself is a number somebody hoped you would not.

So we played 40 million hands at each table, through the same code that deals them in the app, and counted what the house kept.

  • Friendly (single deck, 3:2 on a natural, dealer stands on soft 17): the card said 2%, the hands said 1.99%.
  • Standard (six decks, 3:2 on a natural, dealer stands on soft 17): the card said 2.4%, the hands said 2.34%.
  • Brutal (eight decks, 6:5 on a natural, dealer hits soft 17): the card said 4.1%, the hands said 3.94%.

Friendly was right. The other two were wrong, both by saying the house took more than it does, which is the less embarrassing way to be wrong. It is still wrong on the one screen whose whole point is the number, so the cards now say 2.3% and 3.9%.

What the rules are worth

Friendly and Standard differ only in the shoe: one deck against six. That alone is worth 0.35 points to you. Part of it is naturals: they come a little more often from one deck, and a natural is the only hand that pays more than evens.

Brutal changes three things at once. Eight decks, the dealer hits a soft seventeen, and a natural pays six for five instead of three for two. Together they cost 1.60 points more than Standard. Most of that is the six for five: a natural comes about once in twenty-one hands, and it now pays three tenths of a bet less each time.

Every table here takes more than a casino table with the same shoe and payouts, because doubling and splitting are gone, and both were yours to use. We took them out to keep the game to one decision. The edge on the card is what that decision costs.

How to play it

With only hit and stand, the best play fits in a paragraph. Take a card on 11 or less. Stand on 17 or more. On 12, stand against a dealer 4, 5 or 6 and hit against anything else. On 13 to 16, stand against 2 to 6 and hit against 7 or higher. With an ace counted as eleven, hit 17 or less, hit 18 against a 9, a ten or an ace, and stand on 19 or more.

If you know the usual chart, two things change. A hard 9, 10 or 11 you would double you now just hit, a soft 18 you would double against a 3 to 6 you stand on, and a pair is only its total. A pair of eights is a hard 16, and you hit it against a ten, grimly.

That is the whole strategy the 40 million hands were played with. Play any other way and the house takes more than the card says.

How we counted

scripts/blackjack-edge.ts deals hands through Pip’s Blackjack engine, reshuffles where the app reshuffles, plays each one by the strategy above, and reports the share of each stake the house kept. It ran two separate seeds of 20 million hands a table. Each figure carries a standard error of about 0.016 points, so the first decimal is solid and the second is close.

The strategy was worked out exactly for a shoe with no bottom, where every card is as likely as it was at the start. Over that endless shoe the same strategy loses 2.4% at Standard’s rules and 4.0% at Brutal’s. A real shoe does slightly better for you than an endless one, which is why every dealt figure sits below these.

The count takes three minutes and is not re-run by the test suite. tests/blackjackEdge.test.ts holds the part it can: each card states the edge its table played at, to one decimal, read from src/lib/blackjack/rules.ts.

Where it is

Blackjack is in the membership, with the Friendly, Standard and Brutal tables and their edges on show before you pick one. The chips are play money and are never for sale. It is not poker, and it does not pretend to be.

item.title: Turn-based poker with friends who are never free at once
item.description: A slow game on Pip is a private Hold’em table where each move gets 1 to 24 hours, and your clock stops during your quiet hours. Moves set in advance, a replay of what you missed, and a notification when it is your turn. Any free account can host one at a time; friends join free.
item.content:encoded:
Since this was written (corrected 2 November 2026)

Since 2 November a room opened with a free account has up to four seats and no camera or voice. A member’s room has up to eight, with camera and voice. Friends still join any room free.

Since this was written (corrected 26 October 2026)

Two things below stopped being true within three days. Since 25 October anyone with a free Pip account can host one slow game at a time, and open one live room a day; the membership hosts as many as you like. And since 24 October a slow table has camera and voice, the same as a live room, for when you both happen to be there.

The short version

A slow game is a private Texas Hold’em table where each move gets hours, not seconds. You check on the bus, your friend calls after lunch, the river comes the next morning. Nobody has to be free at the same time, which for most groups of friends is the whole problem.

The host needs the membership. Everybody else needs a free account and the invite. The chips are play chips.

What the host picks

  • 2, 3 or 4 seats, heads-up unless you change it, and no AI players in the empty ones;
  • time for each move: 1, 4, 12 or 24 hours;
  • how it ends: last player standing, after 20, 50 or 100 hands, or on a date, when the hand in play finishes and the biggest stack wins;
  • the stake, starting chips, how fast the blinds climb, and whether the chips come from the Roll or it is just for fun, the same as a live room.

The blinds climb by hands played, not by the hour, so a game that takes a fortnight is not all blinds by the end of it. You can be in 10 slow games at once, which is more than most people have friends who answer.

The clock stops while you sleep

Each player sets their own quiet hours, 23:00 to 08:00 unless they change them, in their own timezone. Your move clock does not run during yours. A one-hour clock that starts at 22:30 has half an hour that night and half an hour after eight the next morning, and the clocks going back in October is handled too. The arithmetic is in src/lib/multiplayer/slow.ts.

Run out of time and Pip checks for you if it can and folds if it can’t. Do that twice in a row and you are sat out, moved for straight away, until you next open the game.

Moves set in advance

While somebody else is thinking, you can set check/fold, check, or call. When the turn reaches you, it is made for you if it still makes sense. A call lapses if the bet changes, and everything lapses when the street ends. Nobody else at the table is told what you set. Live rooms have these now too.

What you missed

Open a game after a day away and the hands you missed play out on the felt, move by move, before you get the table back. There is a Skip. A slow game keeps its last ten hands for this. Each one is dealt again from the moves that were made, and if the replay does not end where the real hand did, it isn’t shown. A wrong replay is worse than none. The rebuild is src/lib/multiplayer/catchUp.ts.

Being told it is your move

Pip asks once, at your first slow game’s table, whether it may send notifications. Say yes and you get one when it is your move. On an iPhone, a browser can only do that once Pip is on your Home Screen.

Email is on unless you turn it off. It comes only if a move has waited a quarter of its clock, or five minutes when there is no device to notify. One email lists every game waiting on you, at most one every twelve hours, and each has a link that turns them off in one tap. Nothing arrives during your quiet hours, or while you have the table open. The rules are src/lib/multiplayer/notices.ts, and the switches are under Settings, Slow games.

What it doesn’t do

It is Hold’em only, there are no cameras at a slow table, and there is no real money and no way to add any. A game nobody starts is cleared after three days, and a finished one stays on Pip’s Home for a week, long enough to mention it to the loser.

Where it is

Opening a slow game is part of the membership, as is opening a live room. Joining a friend’s game is free, and so are the ladder, the Rail, the Daily and the freeroll.

item.title: How often is there a low in Omaha Hi-Lo?
item.description: Six boards in ten allow a low. One hand makes one a little over a third of the time, and ace-deuce a little under half. Counted over every deal, checked against the evaluator that settles Pip’s Hi-Lo pots, and how the odds change with six hands at the table.
item.content:encoded:
Half the pot, if there is a half

In Omaha Hi-Lo every pot is cut in two. The best hand takes one half. The best low takes the other: five cards of different ranks, all eight or lower, the ace counting as one, and still exactly two from your hand with three from the board. If nobody makes a low, the high hand takes the lot.

The description of The Split, Pip’s Hi-Lo table, says nobody makes one about half the time. That is the kind of sentence that gets written once and never checked, so we checked it.

The board decides first

You have to use three board cards for a low, and they have to be three different ranks from ace to eight. A board without them has no low on it for anybody, whatever they hold.

Of the 2,598,960 possible boards, 1,561,728 have three. That is six boards in ten. On the other four, the low half of the game does not happen.

One hand

Then you need two cards of your own, eight or lower, that are not the same ranks as the three you use from the board. Deal one four-card hand and a board every way it can be dealt, 463,563,500,400 ways, and the hand makes a low in 161,374,983,168 of them. A little over one in three.

Even on a board that allows a low, one hand gets there in 161,374,983,168 of 278,557,614,720. Not quite six in ten.

Ace-deuce, and the deuce on the board

Ace-deuce is the low every Hi-Lo player wants to be dealt. Hands holding an ace and a deuce make a low in 13,947,611,904 of 29,650,256,064 deals. A little under half.

The board does most of that. It still needs three different low cards, and they have to be ranks you are not already using. You hold A♠ 2♠ K♦ K♣ and the board comes 2♥ 5♦ 7♣ J♥ Q♠. Three low ranks, so a low is possible. Not for you: your low cards are an ace and a deuce, the board’s are a deuce, a five and a seven, and five different ranks cannot be made from those. Players call that being counterfeited.

Make the 2♥ a 3♥ and the same four cards make 7-5-3-2-A.

More hands, more lows

The question the table cares about is whether anybody makes one, and that depends on how many hands get to the end. We dealt 1,000,000 deals of six hands and a board, everybody staying to the river, and counted the deals where at least one of the first one, two, three hands and so on had a low:

  • One hand: 348,021
  • Two: 495,914
  • Three: 559,220
  • Four: 585,243
  • Five: 595,470
  • Six: 599,126

The first row is a sample of the exact one-in-three above, and lands close to it. Two hands make a low half the time, so “about half” is right heads-up. With six, somebody has one in six deals of ten, and the number cannot climb much further: it is already pressed against the boards that allow one at all. A real table sits somewhere in between, because people fold.

How we counted

A low only cares about which ranks from ace to eight are where, so the exact counts are worked out by rank rather than card by card, which takes under a second. tests/hiLoCounts.test.ts does it on every run and checks that shortcut against src/lib/poker/hiLo.ts, the evaluator that settles the low half at The Split, on twenty thousand dealt hands.

The six-hand rows are a sample, run through that same evaluator with seed 20261020. A million deals take two minutes, too long for the test suite, so they are typed into src/config/hiLoCounts.ts and not re-run.

Where it is

The Split is one of the side tables in the membership, at two stakes. A tap on it there deals a showdown where three kings take the high half, an ace and a three take the low, and a pair of queens wins nothing. The ladder, the Rail, the Daily and the freeroll stay free. So did the counting.

item.title: A poker night with friends, online, with nothing to settle up
item.description: One person opens a private room on Pip and sends a link; everyone else joins free with an account. Up to four seats free, up to eight with camera and voice in a member’s room, and chips that are not money. What the host sets, and what happens when somebody gets up.
item.content:encoded:
Since this was written (corrected 2 November 2026)

Since 2 November a room opened with a free account has up to four seats and no camera or voice. A member’s room has up to eight, with camera and voice. Friends still join any room free.

Since this was written (corrected 26 October 2026)

Below, this post says hosting needs the membership. Since 25 October anyone with a free Pip account can open one room a day, play one quick match a day and host one slow game at a time. The membership opens as many as you like.

The short version

One person opens a private room on Pip and sends the others a link. Up to eight of you sit at one Texas Hold’em table, with your cameras and mics on if you want them. The host needs the membership. Everybody else needs a free account and the link.

The chips are play chips. Nobody owes anybody anything at the end, which used to be the hardest part of the evening.

Who deals

Our server does. It shuffles, deals, and sends each player their own two cards and nobody else’s, until a showdown turns them over. Nobody has to hold a deck up to a webcam and read out the flop. How that works, and the test that checks it, is in Your cards stay on the server.

What the host sets

Before the first hand, the host picks:

  • the seats, from two to eight;
  • the stake, one of the ladder’s, which sets the chips and the blinds;
  • starting chips: standard, deep or very deep;
  • blinds: slow, normal, turbo, or fixed so they never rise;
  • time to act: 15, 30 or 60 seconds;
  • what happens when somebody leaves;
  • whose chips: from the Roll, or just for fun.

Everybody at the table can read the rules. Only the host can change them, and only before the deal. The game is a sit-and-go: the same stack each, the blinds climb unless you fixed them, and the last player with chips wins. The rules live in src/lib/multiplayer/room.ts.

Whose chips

The Roll is the bankroll you carry up Pip’s ladder. From the Roll takes the buy-in from each player’s Roll and pays the winner the buy-in times the seats. Just for fun takes nothing and pays nothing.

Either way the chips are never for sale, and nobody at the table sees anybody else’s Roll or rank. The membership changes nothing once the cards are dealt. A host who pays plays the same cards as a friend who didn’t.

Faces and voices

Both are off until you tap them. Turn the camera on and your face takes your seat where the avatar was. Turn the mic on and the room hears you. The picture is 320 by 240 at 15 frames a second, which is enough to see somebody trying not to smile.

Video and voice go between players’ browsers; the room server passes on the messages that connect them. Tap anybody’s seat to mute them or hide their camera, for you only. Report and block are on the same sheet. A blocked player’s camera and voice stop reaching you, and they are not told.

When somebody gets up

Stand up mid-game and the host’s rule decides. With Keep their seat, your chips stay and your hands fold until you sit back down. With They’re out, you are out after the hand in progress, which is how some poker nights have always ended.

Short of people? Before the deal the host can fill empty chairs with Pip’s regulars, the same characters you meet on the ladder.

What it doesn’t do

It is Hold’em only. There is no real money and no way to add any. A room is cleared half an hour after its game ends, so there is no record of who won last week. You will have to remember that yourselves, and you will.

Where it is

Opening a room is part of the membership, and that page says what else is in it. Joining a friend’s room is free, and so are the ladder, the Rail, the Daily and the freeroll.

item.title: How often both your cards play in Hold’em
item.description: We counted all 2,809,475,760 Hold’em deals. Both hole cards make the best five in 1,324,680,512 of them, a little under half. One card does it more often, and in one deal in twenty the board plays. Worked hands, and when two different fives are both right.
item.content:encoded:
The count

In Hold’em you hold two cards, the board shows five, and your hand is the best five of the seven. Nobody makes you say which five. So we counted how often your own two make it in.

Every way to deal two hole cards and a five-card board from one deck is 2,809,475,760 deals. For each one we took the best hand you can make and asked which of your cards it needs:

  • Both of them: 1,324,680,512.
  • One of them, either will do or only one helps: 1,347,370,964.
  • Neither, because the board alone is as good: 137,424,284.

So both your cards play in a little under half of all deals, and one card does the work slightly more often than two. In about one deal in twenty, your cards play no part at all.

These are deals to the river with nobody folding. Real hands fold, and the ones that get to a showdown are not a random sample. It is a count of what the cards can do, not of what players do with them.

When the board plays

You 8♥ 2♣ · Board 9♠ 10♥ J♦ Q♣ K♠

You have a straight. So does everybody else still in the hand. Your eight makes a straight too, just a worse one, so it sits out. When the board is your best hand, every other player has at least the board as well, and the most you can win is a share.

You 3♣ 3♦ · Board A♠ A♥ K♦ K♣ Q♠

A pocket pair that does nothing. Aces and kings on the board, the queen as the kicker, and your threes are the third pair, which a hand of five has no room for. Three pair has a page of its own.

When one card does it

You A♥ 7♣ · Board K♥ 9♥ 5♥ 2♥ J♠

Four hearts on the board and the ace of hearts in your hand: an ace-high flush. The seven of clubs does not come into it. Swap it for any card but a heart and the hand is the same.

You 6♠ 7♠ · Board 8♠ 9♦ 10♣ K♥ 2♦

Here it takes both. Eight, nine and ten on the board, the six and seven in your hand, and neither card makes the straight without the other.

More than one right answer

You K♥ 9♦ · Board 9♠ 10♥ J♦ Q♣ 3♠

The king makes a nine-to-king straight, and there are two nines to start it with, yours and the board’s. Both fives are the same hand. Neither is more right than the other.

Seven cards can be cut down to five in twenty-one ways, and usually one way is best. Of the 133,784,560 possible sets of seven, 3,079,988 have two or more that tie, about one in 43. Most of them, 2,386,100, are straights with a pair inside them like this one. Another 617,760 are three pair where the third pair is also the best kicker, so either card of it will do. The last 76,128 are full houses and fours of a kind with a spare card to choose between.

How we counted

A short program dealt all 133,784,560 sets of seven and split each one every way it can be split into two hole cards and a board, which takes about a minute. It ranks hands with an evaluator of its own, written for speed, so it is not the code that settles Pip’s pots. Two checks tie it to that code. Its count of each hand type over seven cards matches the standard table exactly. And 400,000 random deals through Pip’s evaluator came out at 19,568 board, 191,959 one card and 188,473 both, against 19,566, 191,832 and 188,602 expected from the full count.

The full count is too slow for the test suite and is not pinned by it. tests/whichFivePlay.test.ts holds the rest: the three rows add up to every deal, and each hand in this post plays the cards it says it does, by Pip’s evaluator.

Where it is

Which five play? is a drill: seven cards, tap the five that count. It is graded by ranking all twenty-one fives, so when two tie, either one is right. It is in the membership. What have you got?, which asks you to name the hand rather than point at it, stays free for everyone, as does Which hand wins?

item.title: Five-Card Draw: what the number of cards gives away
item.description: In Five-Card Draw the only tell is how many cards somebody asks for. Every one of the 2,598,960 five-card hands, dealt through the rule Pip’s Draw regulars throw by, and what each number means.
item.content:encoded:
The only tell

In Five-Card Draw nobody shows a card until the end. There is no board. The one thing you learn about anybody’s hand is how many cards they asked for.

At Pip’s Draw tables, The Parlour, the regulars all decide what to throw by the same short rule, src/lib/poker/ai/draw.ts. A fixed rule turns that number into a read. So we dealt every one of the 2,598,960 five-card hands through it and counted what each number means.

None: they have it

A regular stands pat on a straight or better and on nothing else. That is 19,716 deals, about one in 132. No regular stands pat on a bluff, so when one does, believe it.

One: two pair, or a draw

One card covers three different hands. Two pair throws its odd card: 123,552 deals. Four to a flush throws the fifth: 110,940, and 34,320 of those broke up a pair to do it. Four in a row throws the fifth too: 60,480.

So we dealt the card too: every one of the 47 left, for each of those deals. A little over one in seven ends with a straight or better, the full houses included. About one in three ends with nothing at all, not even a pair. Two pair is still the likeliest thing to come over at the end. One card deserves some respect. Not a lot.

Two: three of a kind, every time

Only trips draw two. 54,912 deals, and nothing else in the rule asks for two. Of all the numbers it is the one that tells you exactly what you are up against.

Three: a pair

The common one, 1,057,224 deals, about four in ten. The rule keeps any pair, deuces included, and throws the rest. Even a pair of twos beats drawing four to an ace, which is what the next number is.

Four and five: nothing

Four cards means an ace and nothing to go with it: 466,560 deals. Five means not even that: 698,880, more than one deal in four. A regular holding K-Q-8-6-3 throws the lot.

The one coin flip

A pair at the end of four in a row, say 5-6-7-8-8, could go either way. The rule keeps the run and draws one 35 times in 100, and keeps the pair and draws three otherwise. It comes up in 6,696 deals, and it is the only spot where the number can mislead you.

What it does not chase

An ace closes a straight at one end. J-Q-K-A fills only with a ten and A-2-3-4 only with a five, four cards rather than the eight that fill 8-9-T-J. The rule chases neither. It keeps the ace and asks for four.

It also misses a pair in the middle of the run. Holding 5-6-6-7-8, it does not see the four in a row, keeps the sixes and draws three.

tests/draw.test.ts holds the rule itself, a hand for each number from standing pat to throwing all five. The counts come from one run over every deal, which takes too long for the test suite, so they are not pinned the way the rule is.

Where it is

The Parlour is one of the side tables in the membership, at two stakes. The page that link opens deals one hand through the draw first, each side throwing by the same rule. The ladder, the Rail, the Daily and the freeroll stay free.

item.title: Your cards stay on the server
item.description: In single-player Pip the whole deck is in your browser. At a multiplayer table that would let anyone read your cards, so our server deals and sends each player only what they may see. The test that checks every step, the one that keeps the AI players honest, and what it does not do.
item.content:encoded:
Since this was written (corrected 2 November 2026)

Since 2 November a room opened with a free account has up to four seats and no camera or voice. A member’s room has up to eight, with camera and voice. Friends still join any room free.

Since this was written (corrected 26 October 2026)

Below, this post says hosting needs the membership. Since 25 October anyone with a free Pip account can open one room a day, play one quick match a day and host one slow game at a time. The membership opens as many as you like.

Two kinds of table

A single-player game of Pip runs in your browser. The deck is in the tab with you, and so are the bots’ cards. Anybody who opens the developer tools can read them. That has never mattered, because the only person you can cheat there is you.

On 11 October Pip got multiplayer: private rooms you open for your friends, and quick match at the ladder’s stakes. Once there is another person at the table, a card in your browser is a card somebody can read.

Face down is only a picture

A card drawn face down is a drawing. If the browser was sent the card, the drawing is all that hides it. So a room is not dealt in anybody’s browser. Our server deals it, and keeps the deck and every hole card.

Each player is sent their own copy of the table, made by src/lib/multiplayer/view.ts. The deck is emptied. Everybody else’s cards are taken out, and only how many each player holds is left, so the backs can still be drawn. Cards come back only for the players a showdown turns over. A pot won when everybody else folds shows nothing to anyone.

Account ids stay on the server too. Nobody at a table needs one, and a list of them is the first thing anyone collecting accounts would want.

Every step, not one hand

A test that checks one hand picked to pass tells you about that hand. tests/multiplayerView.test.ts plays twelve seeded games instead, and at every step checks the copy each person at the table would be sent, and the copy someone watching would get. None may carry the deck, and none may carry a card its reader is not entitled to see.

The AI players

The server does hand its bots the whole table, every card included, which is a fair thing to be suspicious of. The bots’ decisions read their own cards, the board and how everybody has bet. They guess at your hand from your betting, the same way a person would.

We wanted that pinned rather than promised, so tests/multiplayerBotsSeeOwnCards.test.ts makes every bot decision twice in a seeded game: once from the whole table, once from the copy a person in that seat would be sent, with the same dice. The two must match. To check the test could fail, we made a bot look at one opponent’s cards. It failed.

In quick match, AI players take any seat that has not filled after about thirty seconds. Each one has an AI tag on its name plate.

What this does not do

You cannot check a room’s shuffle. The server shuffles, and nothing yet lets you verify it afterwards. The Daily Deal is still the only thing on Pip you can deal again yourself.

The members’ view of the rest of a game after you bust, every hand face up, stays at the single-player tables. At a room the server has nothing to send it.

And none of this makes a room tamper-proof. It means one thing: your cards are not in anybody else’s browser until you show them.

Dealing your friends in

A member opens a room and sends the code. Friends join free with a Pip account, camera and voice if they want them. Multiplayer is part of the membership. The ladder, the Rail, the Daily and the freeroll stay free.

item.title: A beginner beat our hardest table by betting
item.description: The Main Event folded 71% of checked flops to a two-thirds pot bet, where 40% already pays. A player two months into poker found it before we did. What the bots remember now.
item.content:encoded:
The hardest table

The Main Event is the top of Pip’s ladder. Its tagline says near-optimal and merciless. The person who built Pip has played poker for two months, and was beating it, mostly by betting.

That is either good news about the player or bad news about the table. We went to find out which.

Bots against scripts

Pip already had simulations that play the bots against each other. Those can never find a hole every bot shares, because the bot on the other side of the table has the same hole. So we wrote scripts/exploit-sim.ts, which sits a scripted player at a real table against the real bots.

The scripts play the way beginners play. One bets the pot every time it can. One calls everything. One only bets a strong hand. One shoves all-in or folds. One raises every hand it plays and bets every street it is checked to. And one plays the line most people find first: raise a decent hand, bet the flop whatever it brings, bet the turn again if checked to, and give up if anybody fights back.

Seven folds in ten

When that last script raised before the flop and the flop was checked to it, the Main Event folded to a bet of two-thirds of the pot 71% of the time.

A two-thirds pot bet risks two chips to win three. It breaks even if it takes the pot two times in five, which is 40%, and that holds whatever cards you have. At 71% you can make that bet with any two cards and come out ahead before anybody shows a hand.

In 600 tournaments at the Main Event the script won 117. A fair share at six seats is 100.

Why the best bots folded

Every bot read your hand off the chips you had put in. A raise before the flop and a bet after it added up to one of the strongest hands you could hold, whoever made them. That is the right read of somebody who only bets when they have it. It is exactly the wrong read of somebody who bets every time, and the bots could not tell the two apart. They had no memory of who they were playing.

What changed

The bots remember you. src/lib/poker/ai/memory.ts counts, for every player at the table, how often they raise before the flop, how often they bet after it, and how often they fold when bet into. Everybody starts out as a typical player, and a few orbits move the count where one hand cannot. A bet from somebody who bets everything says less, so the bots call it down and raise it back. Against somebody who folds a lot, they bluff more.

The same flop bet now gets folded to 62% of the time from a stranger, and 27% of the time from a player the table has watched bet the pot at every chance.

A bet is read by its size against this street’s pot, with a smaller weight for earlier streets, instead of counting every chip in the hand as proof. That is src/lib/poker/ai/policy.ts.

Short stacks play the chart. At fifteen big blinds or fewer, first in or facing one shove, the strong bots go all-in or fold from the same solved chart Pip’s shove-or-fold drill teaches (src/lib/poker/ai/pushFold.ts). The blinds here climb every few hands, so a lot of a tournament is played that short. The Main Event plays off the chart every time. Lower tables do it less often.

Bet sizes stop giving the hand away from the middle of the ladder up. A bluff there is sized more like a bet for value, and at the top they look the same. The lower tables keep the tell on purpose. A table you can read is where you learn to read.

With all of that in, the same script won 83 of 600 at the Main Event, down from 117.

Then they learned the story

A second change went in the same afternoon. The bots now read the hand as a sequence, not a pile of chips: who raised before the flop, who check-raised, who has led every street. The raiser bets the flop more often. A big hand sometimes checks to the raiser so it can raise later. A seat that has bet every street can finish the bluff on the river. And the table’s count of how often you fold now changes how often it bluffs you.

In 300 tournaments against that table, where a fair share is 50, the c-bet script won 44. The one that bets every street it is checked to won 24.

How sure we are

Six hundred tournaments is not many. A player no better than the table wins 117 or more about one time in 27 by luck alone, so 117 on its own would not have convinced us. The fold rate did. Seven folds in ten against a break-even of four in ten is arithmetic, and a strategy that profits on most flops was always going to show up in the results.

The 44 in 300 says less. A player exactly as good as the table lands there or lower about one time in five, so it says the c-bet stopped winning big, and nothing finer than that. The 24 is a different matter: luck gets that low about once in a hundred thousand tries.

To make 600 tournaments finish, those runs held each bot to 300 simulated hands per decision. The real Main Event thinks through 1,800. And these are scripts, not people. A script does not get bored, change gear or notice that the table has started calling. The real test is a person sitting back down at the Main Event, and that one is open to anybody who gets there.

For the human at the table

Betting all the time works against opponents who do not adjust. Against a table that is watching, a bet that never means anything stops buying folds and starts getting called. The Main Event watches now.

The ladder, the Rail, the Daily and the freeroll stay free. The shove-or-fold drill the bots learned from is in the membership.

item.title: Why a flush beats a full house in Short Deck
item.description: Short Deck throws out the deuces through fives, and the hand order moves to match. Every five- and seven-card hand on a thirty-six card deck, counted by the evaluator that settles Pip’s Short Deck pots.
item.content:encoded:
The rule

Short Deck is Hold’em with the deuces, threes, fours and fives taken out. Thirty-six cards are left, and two rules come with them: a flush beats a full house, and the ace can play low under the six, so A-6-7-8-9 is a straight.

The first one sounds like a house rule somebody lost an argument over. It is arithmetic. Poker ranks hands by how hard they are to make, and on a short deck the flush is the harder one.

Counting them

A full deck deals 2,598,960 different five-card hands. The standard counts are 5,108 flushes and 3,744 full houses, so the flush is the more common hand and ranks below.

A short deck deals 376,992. Of those, 480 are flushes and 1,728 are full houses. Same question, other answer.

We did not look these up. tests/shortDeckCounts.test.ts deals every one of the 376,992 through the evaluator that settles Pip’s Short Deck pots, and fails if a count moves. It also checks that on five cards, from a pair upwards, every hand in the order is rarer than the one below it.

Why the deck does it

A flush needs five cards of one suit. A suit used to have thirteen cards and now has nine, so the ways to pick five from it fall from 1,287 to 126. A full house needs ranks, and every rank left in the deck still has all four of its cards. Stripping the deck costs the full house some company. It costs the flush most of its options.

Seven cards say the same

In Hold’em you play the best five of seven, so we counted those too: all 8,347,680 seven-card hands on a short deck. 633,024 end as a full house and 175,560 as a flush. The flush is still the rarer hand.

The same count found 233,100 that end as nothing at all. On a short deck, seven cards make a full house more often than they make high card. Two pair turns up more often than one pair. It is not a game for anybody who enjoys folding.

That run takes minutes rather than a second, too long for the test suite, so the seven-card counts are not pinned by a test the way the five-card ones are.

Where rarity stops

The order does not follow rarity all the way. It stops at the bottom: on five short-deck cards, nothing at all (122,400 hands) is rarer than a pair (193,536), and nobody has proposed ranking nothing above a pair.

It wobbles in the middle too. On five cards a straight is rarer than three of a kind, 6,120 to 16,128. On seven it is not: 1,169,940 straights against 607,200 sets of trips. In Pip the straight still wins.

Some rooms swap the two for exactly that reason. Pip plays the Triton rules, which is what most players mean by Short Deck: flush over full house, the ace low under the six, and everything else in the usual order. src/lib/poker/shortDeck.ts says which rule set it picked, because choosing quietly between two real rule sets is how a showdown ships wrong.

The ace plays low

With the deuce through five gone, the lowest straight is A-6-7-8-9, the ace standing in below the six. It is a nine-high straight, not an ace-high one, and the difference is a pot: scored as ace high it would beat the ten-high straight it loses to.

The hand library we use for Hold’em reads A-6-7-8-9 as ace high and nothing else, and puts a full house over a flush, without mentioning either. It is the same library we have written about before. So Short Deck has its own evaluator, and tests/shortDeck.test.ts holds both rules, including a check that a short-deck hand is never handed to the library.

Where it is

Short Deck is one of the side tables in the membership, at three stakes. The ladder, the Rail, the Daily and the freeroll stay free. So did the arithmetic.

item.title: Omaha’s exactly-two rule, in five hands
item.description: In Pot-Limit Omaha you hold four cards and must play exactly two with three from the board. Five hands where that changes the answer, checked against the evaluator that settles Pip’s Omaha pots, and how big a pot-limit raise can be.
item.content:encoded:
The rule

In Pot-Limit Omaha you are dealt four cards instead of two. At showdown your hand is exactly two of those four and exactly three of the five on the board. Not one of yours and four of the board. Not three and two. Two and three, every time.

That is the whole difference at showdown, and it is enough to make most Hold’em instincts wrong. Below are five hands, each read twice: once the Hold’em way, best five of seven, and once the Omaha way. Every answer here came out of the evaluator that settles Pip’s Omaha pots, not out of our heads.

Four hearts is not a flush

You hold the ace, king, queen and jack of hearts. The board is 2♥ 7♣ 8♦ 9♠ 10♠.

In Hold’em that is an ace-high flush. In Omaha it is a queen-high straight. Only two of your hearts may play, and a flush needs three more from the board, which has one. The straight is your queen and jack with the 10, 9 and 8.

Neither is one

The other way round. The board is A♥ 9♥ 6♥ 3♥ K♣ and you hold Q♥ 7♠ 4♦ 2♣.

In Hold’em the queen of hearts makes a flush. In Omaha you have ace high and nothing else, because you must use two of your cards and only one of them is a heart. Four to a flush on the board plus one in your hand is the most expensive nothing in the game.

The board is not your hand

The board is 9♣ 9♦ 9♥ 2♣ 2♦: a full house all by itself. You hold A♠ K♦ Q♥ J♠.

In Hold’em everybody plays the board and splits it. In Omaha you have three nines with an ace and a king, since only three board cards play and two of yours must. Anybody with a pair among their four has at least the full house you do not, and the last nine makes four of a kind.

Sometimes the rule gives

The board is 9♣ 9♦ 9♥ 5♣ 2♦ and you hold A♠ A♦ 7♣ 8♦. Nines full of aces, both ways. A pair in your hand is exactly how you use a board with trips on it, and the rule takes nothing off you here.

Two pair is one pair

You hold K♣ K♦ 5♠ 5♥. The board is 6♣ 7♦ 8♥ 9♠ Q♣.

In Hold’em one of your fives finishes a straight. In Omaha that straight would be one of your cards and four of the board’s, which is not allowed. You play the kings with the queen, nine and eight: a pair of kings, on a board where anybody holding a ten and a jack has a straight.

Sixty hands at every showdown

Two of four cards can be chosen six ways. Three of five can be chosen ten ways. So every Omaha player at a showdown has sixty legal hands, and src/lib/poker/handEval.ts builds all sixty and keeps the best. It does not reason about which two cards ought to play, because that reasoning is where Omaha evaluators go wrong, and sixty five-card hands is not much work.

We could have left the reading to the hand library we use. We have written before about what that library does without telling you, so the rule is ours, where a test can hold it. tests/omaha.test.ts deals sixty random hands and checks that each best five is two from the hand and three from the board.

Pot limit

The other half of the name. The most you can raise is the size of the pot after you call. At The Big Pot the blinds start at 25 and 50 and everyone sits with 10,000. First to act before the flop, there are 75 chips in the middle. Calling 50 makes it 125, so you may raise by 125 more: 175 in all. At a no-limit Hold’em table the same seat could put in all 10,000.

The sum is in src/lib/poker/engine.ts, written out, because the usual mistake is to raise by the pot before your call and come up short.

Where it is

Pot-Limit Omaha is The Big Pot, one of the side tables in the membership. The ladder, the Rail, the Daily and the freeroll stay free. The rule was always free to read, and now you have.

item.title: What Google and Apple tell us when you sign in
item.description: Pip accounts can now be made with Google or Apple. Both send us your email and an id, Google adds your name and picture, Apple your name once. We never show or use them.
item.content:encoded:
Two new buttons

The account dialog now offers Continue with Google and Continue with Apple, above the email and password it already had. You press one, go to Google or Apple for a moment, and come back to the page you left, signed in, with your Roll syncing.

An account is still optional. This only changes how long it takes to make one if you want one, which used to be the time it takes to think of a password.

What they hand us

A button that says Continue with Google is also a small data transfer, and the button does not mention it. So here it is, in the same words as the privacy page:

  • Both send your email address and an id for your account with them.
  • Google also sends the name and picture on your Google account.
  • Apple sends your name the first time, and lets you hide your email, in which case we only ever see a relay address Apple makes up for us.

Supabase keeps those with the account record. Pip never shows or uses them: nothing in the app reads the name or the picture, and deleting the account deletes them. We do not need them either. They come with the sign-in.

Two details we cared about more than you will

  • A button only appears once it works. A provider that is not switched on behind the scenes sends whoever presses it to a page of raw JSON on someone else’s domain. So the build lists the providers it offers, and a button is not drawn until its provider is on (src/lib/sync/client.ts).
  • An account made this way has no password, so it does not offer to change one. It says Set a password instead, and setting one lets you sign in with your email as well (src/store/sync.ts).

Neither is interesting. Both are the sort of thing that, done the other way, ends up as a support email.

item.title: Pot odds when you can’t cover the bet
item.description: Facing a bet bigger than your stack, you pay less than the bet and play for less than the pot. Our session review got both halves wrong and called a fold that cost four big blinds a good one. The right sum, worked through one spot.
item.content:encoded:
The short version

There are 500 chips in the middle. Someone bets 1000. You have 300 left. The usual pot odds sum says you pay 1000 to win 1500, so you need a quarter of the pot. That sum is wrong twice over, because you are not paying 1000 and you are not playing for 1500.

Our session review made both mistakes, and the report and the read you get after a hand made the second one. All three are fixed. This is the right sum, and what the wrong one told people.

You call for what you have

A bet bigger than your stack does not cost you the bet. It costs you your stack. Calling puts your 300 in and you are all in, which is what the engine charges and what the Call button already said.

The other 700 of their bet is not yours to win either. Nobody matched it. With one opponent it goes straight back to them; with more, it starts a side pot you have no claim on. What you are playing for is the 500 that was there, plus your 300, plus the 300 of theirs you covered: 1100.

Pot odds are what you put in over the pot you could take, your call included: 300 out of 1100, about 27%. The wrong sum, 300 out of the full 1800, says about 17%. A hand with 20% to win looks like a call on the wrong sum and loses 80 chips on the right one.

What the review said

The review steps back through your session and grades every move at the table, yours and the regulars’, against the cards everyone actually held. For anybody but you it worked out the price from the chips in front of each seat, and it priced a short stack at the full bet, against the full pot.

Take the same spot, blinds at 10 and 20, with the short stack holding 35% against the bettor. The wrong sum takes 35% of a 2500 pot and charges 1000 for it: minus 125. Folding saved 125 chips, so the review marked the fold as good. The right sum takes 35% of 1100 and charges 300: plus 85. The fold gave up 85 chips, about four big blinds. The review told you the opposite of what happened, with a number attached, which is the worst way to be wrong.

The fix is in src/lib/review/moveGrade.ts: call for the smaller of the bet and the stack, and take what nobody could match out of the pot. A test pins the spot above at minus 85.

The report and the read after a hand work from somewhere else: a note the game makes when you act. That note charged you the right 300 and still counted the whole pot, so both judged your short calls on the 17% sum. src/lib/coach.ts now leaves the unmatched chips out. Sessions saved before the fix keep the old note, so the report still grades those spots the old way.

While we were in there

The report that comes with the review had a smaller habit of the same kind. Under You pay off too often at the end, its See the hands list could show a hand you folded, which is a strange way to prove you pay off. Only calls go there now, and folds already saved on your profile are left out when the list is drawn.

Why short stacks

Every venue on the ladder is a tournament, and tournaments end in short stacks. A short stack’s whole hand is often one call. If the number on that call is wrong, there is no second decision to make up for it.

item.title: Deal me in dealt you a menu
item.description: In September, 68 of the 217 people who made a player on Pip did not play a hand within the hour. The tour was not why. The button that said Deal me in opened the lobby, and now it opens a table.
item.content:encoded:
The short version

When you make a player, the next screen offers a short tour or a button that says Deal me in. Until 30 September that button took you to the lobby, which is a lot of things to choose between and none of them a hand of cards. In September, 217 people made a player and 149 of them played a hand within the hour. The other 68 made a character, picked a face for it, and did not play a hand that hour.

Now the button deals you in. It seemed the least we could do, given the name.

It wasn’t the tour

The obvious suspect was the tour, since it sits between making a player and playing. It was innocent. Of the 77 who took it, 52 went on to play a hand. Of the 140 who skipped it, 97 did. Two in three either way, which says people were leaving at the page both routes ended on, and that page was the lobby.

The lobby is fine for someone who knows what the Rail is. For someone who has been a poker player for forty seconds, it is a menu at a restaurant they have not decided to eat at.

What changed

Deal me in, the tour’s Take a seat, and Skip on a tour you started from that screen all go straight to a table now. Which table is the same pick the lobby’s Next up card makes, so the two can’t disagree; for a new player it is Friends’ Garage. That pick lives in src/components/onboarding/firstSeat.ts, which is short. If you haven’t made a player yet, you still go to the page that makes one.

The lobby is still there. You just meet it after you’ve seen a card.

What we don’t know yet

Whether it worked. The numbers above come from our analytics, which count browsers rather than people, over one month. We will read the same step again at the end of October. If it hasn’t moved, the lobby wasn’t the problem either, and we will say so here.

item.title: Pip has a membership now
item.description: £5.99 a month or £49 a year, for multiplayer, the lessons, the drills and more. The ladder, the Rail, the Daily and the freeroll stay free.
item.content:encoded:
The short version

Pip has a membership. £5.99 a month or £49 a year. We waited to write this until a real card had gone through it and come out the other side.

What it buys

The side tables, Pot-Limit Omaha, Short Deck, Omaha Hi-Lo, Five-Card Draw, and blackjack, for some reason. Levels 2 to 5 of Lessons with Webb, every drill, Session review, and the members’ shelf. The full list is on /membership, which is built from the same file the game reads, so it cannot list something that is not built.

What it doesn’t

The ladder, the Rail, the Daily and the freeroll are free forever. Level 1, every written guide, the odds calculator and the per-hand read are free too. Nothing you can buy changes a hand.

On your statement

It is sold by Ava Technologies Global Ltd, so your statement says AVA TECH* PIP. To cancel: Settings, Membership, Manage. We don’t ask why.

item.title: The mock-ups on your landing page are untested claims
item.description: Our home page draws four small pictures of what the game produces. Three were typed out by hand and all three had drifted: a share line missing the address that makes it a loop, a hand permalink six characters long on the card that says there is no server, and an equity read labelled with a phrase the game has never emitted, over a percentage its own caption contradicted. Why the suite stayed green, and the two ways to draw your own output that are true by construction.
item.content:encoded:
Four cards, and a comment at the top of the file

Our home page has four feature cards. Each one carries a small picture of something the game produces: the line you copy after playing the Daily, a shared hand’s link, the win percentage that sits at the table, an avatar with a fan of card backs. They are not images. They are components, laid out in the same design system as the real thing and rendered live on the page, which is why they look right.

The file they live in opens with a comment saying that nothing on the page is a mock-up: what you see here is what you get at the table. That sentence was written when it was true. It stayed in the file for four months, during which three of the four cards drifted away from the product, and the test suite was green every day of it.

The one that did not drift is the difference. It maps over the same config the game reads, so there was nothing in it to get wrong. The other three were typed out by hand next to the code that produces the real version.

One: the share line with the share missing

The Daily card sells the loop. Everyone plays the identical shuffle, so the result line is worth pasting somewhere, and the app appends playpip.io/daily to it so whoever reads it can go and play the same deal.

The card drew that line by hand, from before the address existed. So the card whose entire argument is the share loop displayed the version of the line with the loop cut off, for the month after we shipped it. Not a wrong number. The missing part was the part that made it a mechanism.

The fix is one line: call dailyShareText, the function the app shares with, with fixed arguments. The card now cannot show a line the app would not produce, because it is not drawing a line, it is asking for one.

Two: a link that looked like somebody else's database

The second card says a shared hand needs no server and no account, because the whole hand is folded into the URL fragment. It illustrated that with playpip.io/hand#kQyJ3v….

Six characters and an ellipsis. That is a perfectly normal-looking link, which is the problem: it is what a link looks like when it points at a row in somebody’s database. Short opaque token, server on the other end, gone when the company folds. The picture contradicted the claim it was there to support, and it did it in the visual grammar everyone already reads fluently.

A real one is not like that. We encode the hand as JSON and base64url it, so the length is the hand: every action, every board card, every name, every reveal. The hand now on the card is a six-handed pot that reaches showdown, and it is 566 characters of URL.

the card, at build time

playpip.io/hand#eyJ2IjoxLCJuIjo0MiwiYiI6… (566 characters)

566 characters is not elegant and we are not going to pretend otherwise. It is also the entire point. You can read the hand out of the link with a base64 decoder and no permission from us, and nothing we do later takes a hand away from someone who has the URL. Both numbers in this paragraph are the length of the string in the block above it, because the page computes them at build time. Anything else would be a fourth hand-typed claim in a post about hand-typed claims.

Three: a phrase the game has never said

The third card shows the ambient equity read: how often you win this hand from here, sitting quietly at the edge of the table. The hand-typed version said Top pair, good kicker over 72%, with ahead of 4 in 5 hands underneath.

Three problems, and only the first is the kind you would call a bug.

  • The game has never emitted that label. The readout calls evaluateHand(hole, community).name and prints whatever comes back, which for ace-king on an ace-high flop is the word Pair. Flat, and a bit deflating, and what the product says. Our evaluator also calls a royal flush a Straight Flush, so this is not the first time its naming has surprised us.
  • 72% and four in five are two answers to one question. Four in five is 80%. Whichever was right, the box printed a number and then restated it as a different number, eight points away, in the next line.
  • Neither figure came from a hand. There was no spot behind the card, so there was nothing either number could be checked against. A percentage nobody can reproduce is decoration in the shape of evidence.

The card now names its spot: ace-king on ace-nine-four, three opponents still in. The label is what evaluateHand returns for it. The percentage is 70%, which is where the equity lands (70.20% over 20 runs of 20,000 hands, standard deviation 0.39). The sentence restating it in words is gone, because that sentence was a second claim with nothing under it.

Why the suite stayed green

We have a lot of tests about claims. One walks every page looking for absolutes about money that a paid tier would falsify, because we shipped two of those and served them for sixteen days. One fails if the list of paid drills drifts from the code. We are, if anything, fussy about this.

Two of them walk this exact file. They read every line of the landing page on every run, and they did it while all three cards were wrong, because what they are looking for is a phrase. A banned form of words about money. A sentence that contradicts the roadmap. Miss the phrase and you catch the claim.

A mock is not a phrase. Nobody was ever going to add Top pair, good kicker to a list of sentences we must not write, because until you go and read evaluateHand it is not a false sentence, it is a plausible label. The same goes for a short URL: no string in it is wrong. What is wrong is the relationship between it and a function somewhere else, and grep cannot see a relationship.

That is the generalisable bit, and we do not think it is specific to us. If your marketing page draws your product’s output rather than screenshotting it, you have written claims that no amount of looking for bad sentences will find, in a file that survives every rename and refactor because nothing imports it.

The rule we ended up with

Two ways to draw your own output, and one of them has to be true by construction.

  • Call the function. If something real produces the string, the card asks it for the string with fixed arguments. The Daily line and the hand link both do this now. This is the better option and it is usually available.
  • Or make a test recompute it. Sometimes calling the function is a bad trade: the equity read would drag the hand evaluator and a Monte-Carlo run into the bundle for one card. So the inputs and the expected numbers sit in a config file, the page renders the constants, and a test runs the real thing against them and fails on a gap of more than a point.

The tests are in tests/landingMocks.test.ts. One of them greps the landing page for a typed-out hand link and fails if it finds one, which caught its own author within a minute: we had quoted the old six-character link in a code comment explaining why it was wrong.

There is a fourth card we have not mentioned. It draws a face and three card backs by mapping over the cast and the deck config, which is the same config the game maps over. It has been correct since the day it was written, and nobody has ever had to think about it. That is the whole argument.

item.title: Your Cloudflare Pages site is on Google twice
item.description: Cloudflare noindexes preview deployments and says nothing about the production pages.dev alias, which serves your whole site on a second host. Ours did, for five weeks, with a correct canonical tag on every page. The two-line rule that fixed it, why it is not a redirect, and the test that stops the same file deindexing the real domain.
item.content:encoded:
The host you stopped thinking about

Cloudflare Pages gives every project a pages.dev subdomain. You point a custom domain at it, you tell people the custom domain, and the other one carries on serving. That is the whole bug.

On 26 August 2026 we checked ours from outside. pip-web-9oj.pages.dev returned 200 with the current production build on it, every path, and no X-Robots-Tag of any kind. The site was crawlable on two hostnames, and the copy did not know it was the copy.

The documentation covers the other host

Cloudflare does add the header, and says so plainly: every preview deployment generated by Cloudflare Pages includes the X-Robots-Tag: noindex HTTP response header.

A preview deployment is the per-commit one, at <hash>.pip-web-9oj.pages.dev. The production alias is a different address, it is the one printed in your dashboard, and that page does not mention it either way. So the sentence that sounds like reassurance is about a host you were not worried about. We read it as covering both for five weeks.

The canonical tag was already right, and did not help

Every page on the site carries a canonical pointing at playpip.io, including the pages served on the alias. It was correct the entire time.

It is also not an instruction. Google’s own documentation calls rel="canonical" a strong signal that the specified URL should become canonical, and the page it appears on is upfront that Google decides which version to show. A signal is weighed. A header is obeyed.

On a domain five weeks old with almost no links pointing at it, that difference is the difference between a weak set of ranking signals and two weaker ones. Nobody arrives at your site by ranking twice.

Why it is not a redirect

The obvious fix is a 301 from the alias to the real domain. On Pages a redirect with logic in it means a Function, and the only Function that sees a request for a static file is functions/_middleware.ts at the root. Cloudflare’s docs are specific about what that costs: if you want to run a middleware on your entire application, including in front of static files, create a functions/_middleware.js file.

Entire application includes the host you actually care about. You would be putting a Worker invocation in front of every chunk, image and font on playpip.io in order to tidy up a hostname nobody visits. You can check the hostname and return early inside the middleware, but by then the invocation has happened: that is the part you were trying not to pay for.

public/_headers is read by the CDN, applies per host, and costs nothing at runtime.

The rule

https://pip-web-9oj.pages.dev/*
  X-Robots-Tag: noindex

A _headers pattern written with a scheme and a host matches that host only. playpip.io is untouched, and preview deployments are a third host again and keep the noindex Cloudflare gives them, which is worth preserving: a preview’s permanent address is how you audit a build from outside after something has gone wrong on it.

The same file, one edit later

Now delete the host from that pattern.

/*
  X-Robots-Tag: noindex

The site is gone from search. Every path, on the real domain. The deploy is green, the suite passes, the site opens perfectly for every human being who visits, and there is nothing in the repository a linter or a type checker could object to, because _headers is a text file the CDN interprets after you have shipped it. It is the one file here that can do that, and nothing was reading it.

So something does now. tests/headers.test.ts parses the file the way Pages does, an unindented line being a pattern and the indented lines under it being its headers, and holds one invariant: no rule that sets noindex may match the site itself. It collects the offending rules and compares the list to empty, rather than asserting rule by rule, so it still runs an assertion when the file contains no noindex at all. A test that passes by finding nothing to check is the other way to be green and wrong.

Then break the file three ways and watch, because a test written against a file that already passes has proved nothing about itself. Dropping the host fails two tests. Deleting the whole rule fails one. Taking the noindex line out and leaving the pattern behind fails two others, and the invariant test goes green, which is the right answer: there is no noindex left anywhere to reach anything. It is still executing a comparison at that point rather than skipping an empty loop, and that is the only reason its green is worth reading.

What we cannot tell you

What the duplicate cost us, because we never measured it.
